My father was an occasional mountain climber when he was younger and I grew up hiking (not much real climbing) regularly. Our whole family would take extended camping trips into the Cascades and the Olympic Mountains every summer back in the 1960s. He joined Recreational Equipment Cooperative (REI) when it was just a local Seattle outfit and met Jim Whittaker a number of times at the store. Dad insisted that for our hiking trips we had to be wearing hiking boots with "Bramani soles" — the Vibram brand was just beginning to be used by US manufacturers. At that time those boots were really only available at specialty outlets like REI. Actually I have a vague memory that the first boots he got had to be shipped from Italy.
This guy goes out to the woods, lays on the dirt and bites the ground to bring us the best possible videos. 🧲🐌

Two other things about the iconic Vibram sole pattern: 

It's a really outstanding pattern for outdoor work boots in particular. It holds up well to kicking shovels and stomping, it digs into soft hillsides so you can kick flat steps into a hillside and not have your ankles bent all crazy, and it's very durable; not a lot of teeny tiny features to be ripped off or ground off. They're also very insensitive to dust, mud, and water. 

The other thing is, some of Vibram's soles are so grippy that they're TOO grippy outside of their application. I've had megagrip soles nearly make me trip because they grip so aggressively. The classic pattern is a great balance that's a bit grippier than your foot, but not like having your foot suddenly glued down mid-step.

I first heard about Vibram in the mid '70s, when it was name checked and described for its exceptional qualities in the superb novel The Monkey Wrench Gang, written by Edward Abbey. It was about a loosely connected trio of environmental activists who engage in mayhem and minor vandalism in the American Southwest, and was almost a guidebook about sabotage and general mischief. I was 12 when it came out and very big into environmental issues, and that little detail is strangely one of the only concrete things I remember from the book. 

Soon after I got my first pair of Vasque hiking boots, and was delighted to have that little yellow logo in common with those heroes of my younger self (Danner was unknown in Canada at the time, as far as I remember). They were infamously hard to break in, we treated the thick rough-out leather uppers with neatsfoot oil and protected them with Dubbin. You didn't go on a long hike back then without a piece of moleskin to cut up and stick to your heel or wherever they were needed, but when they did break in they were gloriously comfortable. Looking back now through ads and discussions of vintage boots I can see they were thick Montagna soles, on a leather midsole with a full length leather insole and leather lined. 

There was no Internet then, of course, and there was so much various lore and difference of opinion on the best way to break them in, and treat them. You really depended on the knowledge of the shop you went to, which was usually a Hunting / Fishing one, there were no dedicated hiking and camping ones back then, and most of the other gear we wore was strictly army surplus, all real stuff. 

The smell of wet canvas will forever bring back a flood of memories about those times. On day trips we wore the khaki canvas belts with grommets you could attach your small metal canteen to, that was held in its canvas cover with metal hooks, or you carried the big round one with the woollen insulated cover around your neck or in your pack if you were on a hiking or canoe trip. Shorts were always the wide legged Khaki ones, and the rain gear was a horrible yellow rubber mac, or if you were smart, a waterproof poncho you would wear over your pack. Socks were the classic thick grey wool ones with the red on white band at the top, and we mostly white tees, woollen flannel shirts, Field Jackets, and baseball caps or straw hats. We mostly used canvas flies, tents were rare unless you were in a canoe, even then they were used as little as possible because portaging with them was an absolute bitch. I remember a lot of the stuff rotting away or getting mouldy in storage over the winter, spring was always time for a trip back to the army surplus stores for replacements.
My first taste of  Vibram soles was in the Army, and I haven’t looked back

What you missed in this video, and frankly what a lot of people miss, is a key point about Nike: they're not buying Vibram because it's not Nike's business. Nike is a fashion company. They try to establish fashion trends by courting athletes. They court athletes through high performance products. Nike is not great at high performance technologies - certainly their Beaverton, Oregon campus has a bunch of capabilities to test athletic performance, but it's not their core mission - instead, they want the athletes to wear their brand, and to ensure that they create a story that they have the best products through all of this testing. 

In the end though, at Nike it's not about how well Jordan did with/because of his shoes, it's that Jordan wore those shoes, and that sells the shoes. Nike is only concerned with getting Jordan to wear the shoes, in part by developing a capable shoe, and rigorously protecting their intellectual property for this high performance athletic clothing.
